query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid quench from the melt followed by a controlled annealing just below the eutectic temperature will refine the dual-phase lamellar colonies and improve interfacial cohesion, thereby simultaneously enhancing both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies and numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Rapid quenching from the melt to capture a fine lamellar structure followed by a controlled sub-eutectic annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under ambient pressure; after quenching, the alloy is annealed at a temperature just below the eutectic point (sub-eutectic temperature) for a carefully controlled duration to balance grain refinement and interfacial bonding improvements.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar colony spacing and stronger interfacial cohesion between the dual phases.
generation.mechanism: The rapid quench creates a finer microstructural scale, while the sub-eutectic annealing relieves residual stresses and improves interfacial bonding. This reduces the likelihood of microcrack initiation at the internal boundaries and allows for a more homogeneous deformation, leading to improved strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline produced by conventional processing, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield and fracture strengths with a significant retention or improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility. Exact quantitative improvements are uncertain without experimental validation.
generation.baseline: Conventional processed eutectic high-entropy alloys with as-cast or standard annealed dual-phase lamellar colonies that yield high strength at the expense of limited ductility.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when the alloy composition supports a eutectic microstructure and the annealing temperature is precisely maintained just below the eutectic point. Deviations in cooling rate, annealing temperature, or time could negate the benefits by either coarsening the structure or not achieving sufficient interfacial bonding.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in both tensile strength and ductility remains uncertain until experimentally measured, and the optimal processing window may vary with alloy composition and initial microstructural state.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a representative eutectic high-entropy alloy: one using conventional processing and another using the rapid quench followed by sub-eutectic annealing. Ensure identical composition and casting conditions. Characterize the microstructure using electron microscopy to assess lamellar spacing and interfacial quality, and perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to fracture.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to quantify lamellar colony spacing and interfacial bonding quality
Room-temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation to failure)
Hardness measurements to correlate with tensile properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid quench/sub-eutectic annealing treatment does not produce statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility (or if improvements occur in only one property at the expense of the other) relative to the conventionally processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

The room-temperature strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is relatively low owing to its intrinsic fcc structure. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. It was found that the large and spherical B2 precipitates were generated in the recrystallized grain boundaries of three annealing states, while the small and elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealing state. The former B2 precipitates assisted in refining the recrystallized grains to quasi ultra-fine grain and fine grain regimes (with the grain sizes of ~0.9, ~2.2, and ~7.2 μm). The tensile results indicated that the decreased annealing temperature induced the gradual strengthening of this alloy but also maintained the ductility at the high levels. occupying_moves.conditions: Treatment at temperatures slightly below the eutectic point to relieve residual stresses and modify the dual-phase colony interfaces, conducted under atmospheric conditions that mimic room-temperature tensile performance.

chosen.technique: rapid quenching followed by controlled sub-eutectic annealing
chosen.conditions: The alloy is processed by rapid quenching from the melt to create a fine eutectic structure, followed by an annealing step at a temperature just below the eutectic point. This treatment is performed under ambient pressure and evaluated by room-temperature tensile testing.
chosen.why: This intervention directly inverts the performance limitation that conventional processing tends to enhance strength at the expense of ductility. By carefully controlling the cooling rate and annealing parameters, the treatment refines the lamellar colony spacing and improves interfacial cohesion, thereby reducing microcracking initiation. It builds on standard thermal processing techniques in materials science and is supported by prior evidence highlighting the role of thermal treatments in tuning microstructural features that govern ductility and strength. A falsifying experiment would involve comparing tensile properties of the treated alloy with those of a baseline produced under conventional processing.
